---
title: "Joint probability"
---

The [empirical measure](probability-measures.qmd#the-empirical-measure) assigns
each of the 167 retained token rows mass $1/167$. The probability that two
properties hold of the same sampled token is a [**joint probability**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html). For the
*ne* event $N$ and object event $O$, we write

$$
\mathbb{P}(N,O)
\equiv
\mathbb{P}(N\cap O).
$$

The comma is shorthand for intersection, not an ordering claim: $\mathbb{P}(N,O)=\mathbb{P}(O,N)$.

We compute the four joint cells, recover each marginal by summing the appropriate cells, and then check which denominator each probability uses.

```{r}
#| label: load-joint-data
library(ggplot2)

wh <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/question-core-arguments.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)

stopifnot(nrow(wh) == 167L)

joint_counts <- xtabs(~ ne_lemma + object, data = wh)
joint_probability <- joint_counts / sum(joint_counts)

stopifnot(
  all(joint_counts > 0),
  isTRUE(all.equal(sum(joint_probability), 1))
)

joint_counts
joint_probability
```

The first table contains the four raw counts. Dividing every cell by their
common total, 167, produces the second table. Thus the *ne*–object cell moves
from count 112 to empirical mass $112/167$; the denominator is the entire
sample space because no conditioning has occurred.

## The four joint events

The two binary distinctions partition $\Omega$ into

$$
N\cap O,
\quad
N\cap O^c,
\quad
N^c\cap O,
\quad
N^c\cap O^c.
$$

Their probabilities sum to one because the four events are disjoint and exhaustive:

$$
\mathbb{P}(N,O)
+\mathbb{P}(N,O^c)
+\mathbb{P}(N^c,O)
+\mathbb{P}(N^c,O^c)
=1.
$$

```{r}
#| label: summarize-joint-table
p_ne_object <- unname(joint_probability["1", "1"])
p_ne_subject <- unname(joint_probability["1", "0"])
p_other_object <- unname(joint_probability["0", "1"])
p_other_subject <- unname(joint_probability["0", "0"])

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  p_ne_object + p_ne_subject + p_other_object + p_other_subject,
  1
)))

c(ne_object = p_ne_object,
  ne_subject = p_ne_subject,
  other_object = p_other_object,
  other_subject = p_other_subject)
```

## Marginal probabilities

A **marginal probability** sums over the other distinction. For instance,

$$
\mathbb{P}(N)
=
\mathbb{P}(N,O)+\mathbb{P}(N,O^c),
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}(O)
=
\mathbb{P}(N,O)+\mathbb{P}(N^c,O).
$$

```{r}
#| label: compute-joint-margins
p_ne_from_margin <- sum(joint_probability["1", ])
p_object_from_margin <- sum(joint_probability[, "1"])

stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(p_ne_from_margin, mean(as.logical(wh$ne_lemma)))),
  isTRUE(all.equal(p_object_from_margin, mean(as.logical(wh$object))))
)

c(ne = p_ne_from_margin, object = p_object_from_margin)
```

The two margins do not determine the four cells. They report how common each property is separately but not how the properties co-occur.

```{r}
#| label: plot-joint-probability
#| fig-cap: "Observed joint probability mass for the *ne* and object indicators."
joint_plot <- as.data.frame(joint_probability)
names(joint_plot)[3] <- "probability"
joint_plot$lemma_event <- ifelse(joint_plot$ne_lemma == 1,
                                 "ne", "other lemma")
joint_plot$relation_event <- ifelse(joint_plot$object == 1,
                                    "obj", "nsubj")

ggplot(joint_plot,
       aes(lemma_event, probability, fill = relation_event)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(nsubj = "grey", obj = "steelblue")) +
  labs(x = "Lemma event", y = "Joint probability",
       fill = "UD relation") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The value $\mathbb{P}(N,O)$ is relative to the full finite extract. It does not give the proportion of objects whose lemma is *ne*, because that question uses only the object event as its reference set. The [next page](conditional-probability.qmd) changes the denominator explicitly.

The treebank's sentence sampling and annotation process remain part of the interpretation. These joint probabilities summarize the retained annotated tokens; they do not estimate a context-free grammar of Turkish interrogatives.

## Check your understanding

1. Use `joint_probability` to compute $\mathbb{P}(N^c,O)$ and interpret it.
2. Verify both marginalization identities in R.
3. Why does $\mathbb{P}(N,O)$ not mean “the proportion of object tokens that are *ne*”?
4. Construct the three-by-two lemma–relation joint table directly from `wh` and verify that its cells sum to one after normalization.
5. A student divides every cell by its row total and calls the result a joint
   PMF. What distribution has actually been computed?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. $\mathbb{P}(N^c,O)=4/167=0.023952$, the probability that a uniformly sampled retained token is an object with a lemma other than *ne*. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Summing the *ne* row gives $147/167=0.880240$, and summing the object column gives $116/167=0.694611$, matching the two direct marginals. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. $\mathbb{P}(N,O)$ divides the 112 joint tokens by all 167 retained tokens, whereas the proportion of object tokens that are *ne* divides 112 by the 116 object tokens. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The normalized lemma-by-relation cells are 2, 1, 14, 3, 35, and 112 divided by 167, and their probabilities sum to $(2+1+14+3+35+112)/167=1$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. Row normalization produces conditional relation probabilities within each
   lemma, not joint probabilities over the full extract.

</details>

The four-cell count table, joint PMF, and margins are three representations of
the same co-occurrence structure. Dividing each cell by 167 converts counts to
joint probabilities, and summing the resulting rows or columns recovers the
margins. The [next page](conditional-probability.qmd) changes the denominator
to a selected reference event.
